lesson.lesson_summary: Every word in a sentence has a job. These jobs are called parts of speech. Learn the eight traditional parts of speech, understand what each one does, recognise them in sentences, and use them correctly.

learning_objectives.description: Explain what parts of speech are and why they are important.
success_criteria: Explain that parts of speech describe the jobs words do in sentences.
Recognise that different words can perform different grammatical jobs.

learning_objectives.description: Identify and describe the eight traditional parts of speech.
success_criteria: Name all eight parts of speech.
Explain the basic function of each part.
Give an appropriate example of each part.

learning_objectives.description: Recognise the parts of speech used in sentences.
success_criteria: Identify nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections.
Explain the grammatical function of an identified word in its sentence.

learning_objectives.description: Understand how the eight parts of speech work together.
success_criteria: Explain how different word classes contribute to sentence meaning.
Recognise how a word's grammatical role depends on its use in a sentence.

learning_objectives.description: Distinguish between commonly confused parts of speech.
Apply knowledge of parts of speech to understand and construct simple sentences.
success_criteria: Choose appropriate word classes to complete sentences.

pages.title: Every Word Has a Job

content.text: Look at a sentence. Every word helps us share an idea. Some words name things. Some show actions. Others describe things or connect ideas. Each word has a job.

examples.explanation: Rita names someone, sings shows an action, and beautifully tells us how she sings.

pages.key_takeaway: Words have different jobs in sentences.

pages.title: What Are Parts of Speech?

content.text: Parts of speech are groups of words. We group words by the jobs they do in a sentence. English has eight traditional parts of speech.

content.title: Think of a team
content.text: A football team has players with different jobs. Words also have different jobs when they work together.

examples.explanation: Different words perform different jobs to build one meaningful sentence.

pages.key_takeaway: The job of a word helps us identify its part of speech.

pages.title: Meet the Eight Parts

content.text: There are eight traditional parts of speech. Each group has a special job. Let's meet them one by one.

content.introduction: The eight parts of speech are:
items: Verb – shows an action or state.
Adjective – describes a noun or pronoun.
Adverb – modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
Preposition – shows a relationship between words.
Conjunction – joins words or groups of words.
Interjection – expresses a sudden feeling or reaction.

pages.key_takeaway: Remember all eight: Noun, Pronoun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, Preposition, Conjunction and Interjection.

pages.title: Noun – Naming Words

content.text: A noun names a person, place, animal, thing or idea. It tells us who or what we are talking about.

examples.explanation: Maya names a person. School names a place.

examples.sentence: The dog plays with a ball.
examples.explanation: Dog names an animal. Ball names a thing.

pages.key_takeaway: A noun names someone or something.

pages.title: Pronoun – Replacement Words

content.text: A pronoun is a word used instead of a noun or noun phrase. It helps us avoid repeating the same name again and again.

examples.sentence: Riya is my friend. She is kind.
examples.explanation: She is a pronoun. It refers to Riya.

examples.sentence: The boys are playing. They are happy.
examples.explanation: They is a pronoun that refers to the boys.

pages.key_takeaway: A pronoun can take the place of a noun or noun phrase.

pages.title: Verb – Action and State Words

content.text: A verb tells us what someone or something does, or what state it is in. Action verbs show activities. Other verbs express states or help other verbs.

examples.explanation: Kicks tells us what Tom does.
Is connects Sara with her state of being.

pages.key_takeaway: Verbs express actions, states or help other verbs.

pages.title: Adjective – Describing Words

content.text: An adjective describes a noun or pronoun. It gives us more information about a person, place, animal or thing.

pages.key_takeaway: An adjective gives more information about a noun or pronoun.

pages.title: Adverb – Modifying Words

content.text: An adverb adds information to a verb, an adjective or another adverb. It can tell us how, when, where or how often something happens.

examples.explanation: Beautifully tells us how the girl sings.
Very adds information about the adjective tall.

pages.key_takeaway: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.

pages.title: Preposition – Relationship Words

content.text: A preposition shows how one word relates to another. It often tells us about place, time, direction or position.

examples.sentence: The cat is under the table.
examples.explanation: Under shows where the cat is in relation to the table.

pages.key_takeaway: A preposition shows a relationship between words.

content.text: A conjunction joins words or groups of words. An interjection expresses a sudden feeling or reaction.

items.label: Conjunction
items.description: Joins words or groups of words.

items: Conjunctions: and, but, or, because, although

pages.title: Find the Word's Job

content.text: To identify a part of speech, look at how a word is used in its sentence. Ask what job the word is doing. Do not identify it by its spelling alone.

examples.explanation: Happy is an adjective, child is a noun, laughs is a verb, and loudly is an adverb.

items: Does it replace a noun? Pronoun.
Does it show an action or state? Verb.
Does it describe a noun or pronoun? Adjective.
Does it modify a verb, adjective or adverb? Adverb.
Does it show a relationship? Preposition.
Does it join words or groups? Conjunction.
Does it express a reaction? Interjection.

pages.key_takeaway: Look at the word's job in the sentence.

pages.title: Explore One Sentence

content.text: Let's look at how several parts of speech work together in one sentence.

examples.sentence: Wow! The little boy runs quickly through the garden.
examples.explanation: Wow is an interjection, the is an article traditionally classified as an adjective in some school grammar systems, little is an adjective, boy is a noun, runs is a verb, quickly is an adverb, and through is a preposition.

content.title: A useful detail
content.text: Modern grammar usually treats articles such as the and a as determiners, rather than adjectives. The traditional eight-part classification is a simplified school grammar framework.

pages.key_takeaway: A sentence can contain several different parts of speech.

pages.title: Adjective or Adverb?

content.text: Adjectives describe nouns or pronouns. Adverbs can describe actions and give more information about adjectives or other adverbs. They do different jobs.

items.label: Adverb
items.description: Modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.

comparison_points: Carefully tells us how she drives.
content.conclusion: Check what the word describes before deciding its part of speech.

pages.key_takeaway: Adjective describes a noun or pronoun. Adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb.

pages.title: Words Can Change Jobs

content.text: A word does not always belong to the same part of speech. Its job can change when we use it differently in a sentence.

comparison_points: In the first sentence, book names a thing.
In the second sentence, book describes an action.
content.conclusion: The same spelling can have different grammatical jobs.

mistake.incorrect: Every word ending in -ly is an adverb.
mistake.correct: Check the word's function in the sentence.
mistake.reason: Many adverbs end in -ly, but some adjectives, such as friendly and lovely, also end in -ly.

pages.key_takeaway: Identify words by their function, not just their appearance.

content.text: Now use what you have learned. Look carefully at each word and think about its job. Choose the correct answer.

pages.title: You Know the Eight!

content.text: Great work! You have learned the eight traditional parts of speech. Remember that each word has a job, and its job helps us understand the sentence.

items: Verb – shows an action or state.
Adjective – describes a noun or pronoun.
Adverb – modifies a verb, adjective or adverb.

content.title: Remember this
content.text: Do not just look at a word. Look at the job it does in the sentence.

pages.key_takeaway: Eight parts of speech help us understand how English sentences work.

question_bank.prompt: What do parts of speech tell us?

options.text: The jobs words do in sentences
The number of letters in words
The number of sentences in a paragraph

question_bank.explanation: Parts of speech group words according to their grammatical jobs in sentences.

question_bank.prompt: Which list contains all eight traditional parts of speech?

options.text: Noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection
Noun, verb, number, colour, sentence, paragraph, article, question
Noun, pronoun, tense, voice, mood, verb, phrase, clause
Verb, noun, adjective, punctuation, spelling, letter, sound, paragraph

question_bank.explanation: These are the eight traditional parts of speech in English grammar.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the part of speech of the highlighted word: 'The teacher smiled.' Highlighted word: teacher.
question_bank.explanation: Teacher names a person, so it is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: In 'The baby sleeps peacefully', what is the part of speech of peacefully?
question_bank.explanation: Peacefully tells us how the baby sleeps. It modifies the verb sleeps, so it is an adverb.

question_bank.prompt: Choose the correct part of speech for 'and' in 'Ravi and Mina are friends.'
question_bank.explanation: And joins the two names Ravi and Mina. It is a conjunction.

question_bank.prompt: Which word is a pronoun?
question_bank.explanation: They is a pronoun that can refer to people or things.

question_bank.prompt: Which word is an adjective in 'The clever girl won'?
question_bank.explanation: Clever describes the noun girl.

question_bank.prompt: Which word is a preposition in 'The keys are on the table'?
question_bank.explanation: On shows the relationship between the keys and the table.

question_bank.prompt: Which word is an interjection?
question_bank.explanation: Wow! expresses surprise or excitement.

question_bank.prompt: A verb can express a state, not just an action.
question_bank.explanation: Correct. Verbs such as know, love and believe express states.

question_bank.prompt: Which sentence uses 'book' as a verb?
question_bank.explanation: In this sentence, book means to arrange or reserve something. It expresses an action, so it is a verb.

question_bank.prompt: Which statement about words ending in -ly is correct?

options.text: Many adverbs end in -ly, but some adjectives also do.

question_bank.explanation: Carefully is an adverb, but friendly and lovely are adjectives. Function matters more than spelling.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the part of speech of 'quickly' in 'The rabbit jumps quickly'.
question_bank.explanation: Quickly tells us how the rabbit jumps. It modifies the verb jumps.

question_bank.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'The children play ___ the park.' Choose a suitable preposition.
question_bank.explanation: In shows the place where the children play.

question_bank.prompt: Which word completes the sentence with a conjunction? 'I wanted to play, ___ it was raining.'
question_bank.explanation: But joins two contrasting ideas.

question_bank.prompt: What is the main purpose of learning parts of speech?

options.text: To understand how words work in sentences

question_bank.explanation: Understanding parts of speech helps us recognise how words build meaningful sentences.

question_bank.prompt: Match each part of speech with its main job.

right_items.text: Modifies a verb, adjective or adverb
Joins words or groups of words

question_bank.explanation: Each part of speech has a different grammatical job. Match the word class to its function.

question_bank.prompt: In 'She sings beautifully', what is the part of speech of 'She'?
question_bank.explanation: She is a pronoun that refers to a person without repeating their name.

question_bank.prompt: Which sentence contains an adjective?
question_bank.explanation: Red describes the noun car, so it is an adjective.

question_bank.prompt: In 'The children sat under the tree', what does 'under' do?

options.text: Shows the relationship between the children and the tree

question_bank.explanation: Under is a preposition showing the position of the children in relation to the tree.

question_bank.prompt: Which sentence uses an interjection correctly?

options.text: Wow! That is a beautiful painting.

question_bank.explanation: Wow expresses a reaction of surprise or admiration.

final_assessment.title: The Eight Parts of Speech – Final Check

cross_references.reason: The lesson introduces nouns and gives examples but does not comprehensively teach common, proper, collective, abstract and other noun classifications.
Common pronouns are introduced, but personal, possessive, reflexive, demonstrative, relative and other pronoun classifications require separate teaching.
Action, state and helping verbs are introduced. Detailed classifications such as transitive, intransitive, linking, regular and irregular verbs require separate lessons.
Descriptive functions are introduced, but positive, comparative and superlative forms are not taught.
Examples of place, time, direction and position are introduced without comprehensive teaching of prepositional phrases and usage rules.
Common conjunctions are introduced, but coordinating, subordinating and correlative conjunctions require separate teaching.
Articles are mentioned to clarify the difference between traditional school grammar and modern grammatical classification. Their complete functions and classifications require a separate lesson.
The lesson uses simple sentences to demonstrate word functions but does not comprehensively teach sentence elements, phrases or clauses.

issues_found: The actual Learn Lesson JSON Schema v2.0 file was not supplied separately. The structure has been prepared against the output contract in Lesson Generation Prompt v2.0, but strict machine validation against the canonical schema remains necessary.
The eight parts of speech are presented using the traditional school grammar framework. Modern grammatical frameworks classify some words, especially articles, differently.
The lesson introduces the eight word classes but intentionally leaves their detailed sub-classifications to separate lessons.
corrections_made: Separated all eight traditional parts of speech into individual teaching pages or a clearly focused combined page for conjunctions and interjections.
Added examples demonstrating the grammatical function of each word class.
Added a clarification about articles and modern determiner classification.
Included examples showing that the same spelling can perform different grammatical functions in different sentences.
Added a warning against identifying all words ending in -ly as adverbs.
Separated dimension assessment questions from final assessment questions.
Checked question references, answer keys, objective references, example highlights and matching-pair identifiers.
